newsitem.title: USA: Arguments to begin in La. breast implant trial.
newsitem.headline: Arguments to begin in La. breast implant trial.

text.p: Opening arguments are set for Wednesday in the first phase of a class-action lawsuit in which up to 10,000 Louisiana women seek damages from companies that manufactured, tested or sold silicone breast implants.
It took more than a week for attorneys to pick 12 jurors and six alternates for the trial, which is expected to last six to eight weeks.

Orleans Parish District Civil Judge Yada McGee ruled earlier that in this phase, involving an estimated 1,700 plaintiffs, the jury will decide if Dow Chemical Co. bears any responsibility for testing silicone as a medical device. Dow Chemical is half owner of the bankrupt implant manufacturer Dow Corning.
Jurors also will decide if the company failed to disclose, or even suppressed, information on risks and if that kept recipients from making an informed decision about silicone breast implants.

Dow Corning was dismissed from the lawsuit because of bankruptcy proceedings. All claims against it will be handled by U.S. Bankruptcy Court. The case against Bristol-Myers Squibb Co., another manufacturer, will be tried later.

If the jury determines that Dow Chemical bears some reponsibility for testing and safety, the trial will go into the second phase in which the same jury will be asked to decide if silicone caused injuries, if the recipients were aware of the risks, and if they would have received the implants had they known about all of the dangers.

The third step, if the jury decides that silicone caused medical problems, would be to notify potential class members. Another trial with a new jury would be held after grouping class members with similar illnesses. Class members would have to prove they would not have had the implants except for misrepresentations.

Lead plaintiffs' lawyer Dawn Barrios said the key issue is Dow Chemical's responsibility for testing silicone and component parts for Dow Corning, which had no toxicology lab and relied on Dow Chemical for safety information.
She said scientists had discovered as early as the 1950s that silicone migrates to the brain, liver and spleen and could be highly toxic.

Dow officials maintain the suit was filed for plaintiffs trying to obtain financial compensation only because the company has "deep pockets." Spokesman John Musser told Reuters the company was nothing more than a shareholder in Dow Corning and its silicone testing was unrelated to breast implants.
The company also maintains there is no scientific proof that silicone implants cause medical problems.

An estimated 1 million American woman have received breast implants, about 80 percent of them for cosmetic reasons. Several thousand say they suffered serious immune system and connective tissue disorders after the implants leaked or ruptured.
About 300,000 women received Dow Corning implants between 1962 and 1992, when the company ceased manufacturing them.
